s: Forbes real-time billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026: $2.6B, rank #1628
m: Published list figure; Forbes marks his holding at roughly 6% of CoreWeave
did: Co-founded CoreWeave in 2017 with Michael Intrator and Brian Venturo, three commodity traders who bought Nvidia GPUs to mine ethereum, then repointed the fleet at AI training after the crypto crash. CoreWeave listed in March 2025 near a 23 billion dollar valuation and signed a 14 billion dollar Meta compute deal.
why: They physically owned GPUs at the moment ethereum stopped needing them and ChatGPT created a compute shortage the hyperscalers could not fill. Nvidia allocated scarce H100s to CoreWeave precisely because it was not a competing cloud, and take-or-pay contracts from Microsoft and OpenAI let them finance more chips against the contracts.
obst: The 2018 ethereum collapse left them holding thousands of depreciating cards and no business; they rented them to visual-effects and drug-discovery shops for pennies to survive. Short sellers later argued the billions in high-yield GPU-backed debt could not be serviced through a hardware refresh cycle.
turn: Nvidia's 2023 decision to invest in CoreWeave and allocate it scarce H100 capacity, which turned a mining leftover into the default AI cloud.

s: Forbes 2026 Billionaires list via the Utah state ranking, June 2026: $3.3B
m: Published list figure
did: Started Qualtrics in his parents Provo basement in 2002 with his father Scott and brother Jared, selling survey software to university researchers. Sold it to SAP for 8 billion dollars in 2019, re-listed it in 2021 and sold again to Silver Lake for 12.5 billion in 2023. Bought the Utah Jazz in 2020.
why: Qualtrics landed with professors first, who taught it to students who then specified it at work, so an academic beachhead converted into enterprise seats without a sales force. Bootstrapping for eleven years before taking a dollar of venture money meant the family still held most of the equity when SAP bid.
obst: They refused outside capital until 2012 and were criticised for it; the company had already filed to go public when SAP appeared, and the founders had 96 hours to choose. His father's throat cancer diagnosis in 2002 was the reason the family started the business together at all.
turn: SAP's January 2019 pre-emptive 8 billion dollar bid, made four days before the IPO was due to price.

s: Forbes real-time profile, 21 Aug 2026: $4.8B, rank #886
m: Published list figure
did: Co-founded Marvell Technology in a Silicon Valley living room in 1995 with her husband Sehat Sutardja, building the read-channel chips inside hard drives and later Wi-Fi and Ethernet controllers; IPO'd in 2000. Forced out in 2016, she moved to Las Vegas, where Nevada levies no income tax, and backed MeetKai and Silicon Box.
why: Marvell sold the one mixed-signal chip every disk-drive maker needed and none wanted to design in-house, then reused that analogue expertise in wireless and networking. As the only woman co-founder of a US chip company she ran sales and operations while the Sutardjas designed, so customer and silicon decisions sat in one household.
obst: An internal accounting review of revenue recognition pushed her and her husband out of their own company in 2016; no fraud was ever found. Marvell had earlier lost a 1.17 billion dollar patent verdict to Carnegie Mellon. Her husband died in 2024.
turn: Winning Seagate's read-channel socket in 1997, which made Marvell the default supplier to the entire disk-drive industry.

s: Forbes real-time profile, 21 Aug 2026: $3.1B, rank #1366
m: Published list figure for one of four Love siblings each marked at $3.1B
did: Chief culture officer and executive vice president of Love's Travel Stops, the 600-plus site truck-stop chain her parents Tom and Judy Love began in 1964 with a 5,000 dollar loan and a leased filling station in Watonga, Oklahoma. The private company now turns roughly 22 billion dollars a year; her brothers Frank and Greg are co-CEOs.
why: Love's bought and built its own real estate on interstate exits before the corridors filled in, then stacked high-margin restaurant franchises, tyre care and truck servicing on top of low-margin diesel. Staying private let the family plough every dollar of cash flow back into land instead of paying dividends.
obst: The chain nearly failed in the 1970s oil shocks when federal gasoline allocation rules capped what independent stations could buy, and the family sold stores to survive. Family succession across three generations has broken comparable chains.
turn: The early 1980s decision to convert from gas stations into full interstate truck stops, betting the family on deregulated trucking and diesel.

s: Forbes real-time profile, 21 Aug 2026: $2.5B, rank #1689
m: Published list figure for a private company with roughly $1.8B of annual sales
did: Third-generation owner of Greater Omaha Packing, the beef plant his grandfather started in 1920 killing one steer a day. He took it over in 1987 and grew it roughly tenfold into the fifth-largest US beef processor, about 1.8 billion dollars of sales, shipping to 69 countries and to restaurants including The French Laundry.
why: He kept one Omaha plant instead of scaling nationally, which let him sort carcasses by quality and sell branded premium and export cuts at prices the four big packers commodity chains cannot match. Writing the plant's own billing and operations software in 1980 gave him lot-level traceability decades before buyers demanded it.
obst: Cattle-cycle margin swings that bankrupt independents, the 2020 covid outbreaks that shut packing floors, and repeated export bans after BSE and E. coli scares that closed whole countries to American beef overnight.
turn: Winning Japanese and Korean export approval in the 1990s, which turned Omaha chuck and short rib into premium branded product.

s: Forbes real-time profile, 21 Aug 2026: $2.1B
m: Published list figure; Forbes marks his stake near 4% of Axon after option exercises and sales
did: Founded TASER International in a Scottsdale garage in 1993 after two high-school friends were shot, took it public in 2001, then remade it as Axon in 2017 around body cameras and the Evidence.com cloud. A 2018 performance option package worth 8% of the company is what made him a billionaire.
why: Giving the camera away cheaply and charging a recurring per-officer subscription for evidence storage converted a hardware vendor into a SaaS business with switching costs measured in petabytes of chain-of-custody video. Departments buy on multi-year budget cycles, so once on Evidence.com they effectively never leave.
obst: Product-liability suits blamed the taser for in-custody deaths through the 2000s and the stock collapsed after a 2005 SEC inquiry into distributor sales. He then gave every US patrol officer a free body camera for a year, deliberately destroying near-term hardware revenue.
turn: The 2017 decision to give away cameras and rename the company Axon, trading hardware margin for subscription lock-in.

s: Forbes 2026 Billionaires list via the Oklahoma state ranking: $1.8B
m: Published list figure
did: Founded Paycom in Oklahoma City in 1998 with about 1.5 million dollars raised on credit cards and from local backers, building one of the first payroll systems delivered entirely over the internet. Took it public on the NYSE in 2014 and into the S&P 500 in 2020.
why: One database for payroll, HR, time and benefits meant no reconciliation between modules, and pushing data entry onto employees themselves cut service cost per client. Building it in Oklahoma City kept engineering and sales wages far below what ADP and Workday paid on the coasts.
obst: Early clients would not put payroll in a browser and he sold door to door for years. In 2023 the Beti self-service product cannibalised Paycom's own service revenue on purpose, growth guidance was cut, and the stock fell by more than half.
turn: The April 2014 Nasdaq IPO, which financed a national outside-sales build-out from a standing start.

s: Forbes individual profile of $1.7B, last marked March 2016; the J.R. Simplot Company is private
m: Dated Forbes estimate carried forward unchanged rather than re-modelled, because the company discloses nothing
did: A director and one of the four children of J.R. Simplot who own the Boise potato, fertiliser and phosphate group. She shares control with her brother Scott, who chairs it. The company supplies roughly a third of America's frozen french fries and turned about 9.8 billion dollars of sales in 2023.
why: Her father patented the frozen fry in 1953 and signed McDonald's in 1967, so Simplot volume grew with a hamburger chain's store count rather than with grocery demand. Owning phosphate mines let the company sell fertiliser to the same growers whose potatoes it bought, capturing both ends of the same field.
obst: The family had to hold a private company together against estate-tax pressure to sell or list after J.R. Simplot died in 2008, then rode out the 2015 collapse in phosphate prices and the covid closure of the restaurant channel that eats most of its fries.
turn: The 1967 handshake with Ray Kroc that made Simplot the fry supplier to McDonald's.

s: Forbes real-time profile, 21 Aug 2026: $1.5B
m: Published list figure, built on the disclosed $1.17B FirstCash consideration and a retained 9% FirstCash stake
did: Founded American First Finance in Wichita in 2013, underwriting lease-to-own and retail instalment plans for shoppers rejected by prime lenders at furniture, tyre and mattress stores. Sold it to pawn operator FirstCash in December 2021 for about 1.17 billion dollars in cash and stock and kept roughly 9% of the buyer.
why: He wrote credit at the point of sale for merchants whose customers had no other financing, so an approval converted a sale the retailer would otherwise lose entirely. The merchant, not the borrower, was the customer, and virtual lease-to-own scaled across thousands of independent stores without opening a single branch.
obst: Lease-to-own pricing draws state attorneys general and CFPB scrutiny that can void a whole state's book, and the business runs on warehouse credit lines that reprice the moment funding tightens. He built it in Wichita, a thousand miles from the capital that funds specialty lenders.
turn: The December 2021 sale to FirstCash, which converted a private receivables book into cash and listed equity.

s: Forbes real-time profile, 21 Aug 2026: $1.2B
m: Published list figure for her share of the 90% Leprino Foods stake inherited in June 2025
did: Inherited with her sister Terry the 90% of Leprino Foods left by their father James Leprino when he died in June 2025. The Denver company her grandfather started as a corner grocery in 1950 is the world's largest mozzarella maker, producing over a billion pounds a year for Domino's, Pizza Hut and Papa John's.
why: Leprino tied itself to the pizza chains national rollouts and then engineered mozzarella specifically for delivery, cheese that still browns and stretches after twenty minutes in a car. Siting plants next to dairy herds in California, New Mexico and Michigan cut the cost of hauling milk, which is mostly water.
obst: The company depends on a handful of pizza customers who could dual-source, and it fought a long trade-secrets battle over its whey processing. The 2025 succession handed a business that had one decision maker for fifty years to two heirs with no operating role.
turn: Winning Pizza Hut's national mozzarella contract in the 1980s, which made a Denver cheesemaker the pizza industry's default supplier.

s: Forbes profile, marked 10 March 2026: $1.1B
m: Published list figure for his share of the Sands family holding in Constellation Brands
did: A Sands family heir to Constellation Brands, the wine and beer group his grandfather Marvin Sands started in 1945 as a bulk wine business and which now owns the perpetual US rights to Corona and Modelo. The family took about 1.5 billion dollars pre-tax in 2022 when it gave up its supervoting shares. He lives in Jackson, Wyoming.
why: The fortune turns on one asset: the perpetual US import and production rights to Corona and Modelo, bought from Anheuser-Busch InBev for 4.75 billion dollars in 2013 when antitrust regulators forced a divestiture. Mexican beer then outgrew every other US beer category for a decade while domestic lager shrank.
obst: Governance investors attacked the dual-class structure for years; converting it in 2022 closed the discount but ended the family's veto over its own company. Wine brands bought at the top of the 2010s were written down and dumped to Gallo, and the 2024 cannabis write-off of Canopy Growth cost billions.
turn: The June 2013 forced divestiture that handed Constellation Corona and Modelo outright rather than as a licensee.

s: Boyd Gaming DEF 14A filed 20 Mar 2026: 13,458,815 shares, 17.87% of class; BYD closed $80.78 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times fetched market price; excludes any non-Boyd Gaming assets
did: Became chairman of Boyd Gaming on 1 January 2026 after 36 years on the board of the company her father William and grandfather Sam Boyd built from the 1975 California Hotel into 28 casinos. She is the largest individual shareholder at 17.87% and drove the locals-casino strategy that defines Boyd in Las Vegas.
why: Boyd targets Las Vegas residents rather than tourists, building neighbourhood casinos with cheap food and dense slot floors that fill on a Tuesday. Locals play year-round and do not stop when conventions cancel, so Boyd's cash flow survived downturns that emptied the Strip.
obst: The Echelon tower on the Strip was halted in 2008 with billions committed, leaving a hole in the ground for a decade, and the debt from the Coast Casinos and Ameristar deals arrived just before the crisis. New Jersey regulators forced partner MGM to divest its half of Borgata.
turn: The 2003 opening of Borgata in Atlantic City, a 50-50 venture with MGM that became the highest-grossing casino in the market.

s: Forbes 400 listings in the mid-2000s at roughly $1.0-1.3B, plus the disclosed $1.2B sale of 130 hotels to Goldman Sachs Whitehall in 2006
m: Dated national rich-list figure carried against documented sale proceeds and the later Tharaldson Ethanol build; no current published figure exists
did: A North Dakota schoolteacher who built roughly 400 limited-service hotels, Super 8, Comfort Inn and Fairfield Inn, mostly on interstate exits in small Midwest cities, then sold 130 of them to Goldman Sachs Whitehall funds for about 1.2 billion dollars in 2006 and put the proceeds into a 175-million-gallon ethanol plant at Casselton.
why: He standardised one building design and self-performed the construction, so each hotel cost far less per room than a franchisee paying a general contractor. Building in secondary markets meant no bidder for the site and franchisors happy to grant territory nobody else wanted.
obst: The post-2001 travel collapse fell hardest on limited-service hotels dependent on business drive-through traffic, and the Casselton ethanol plant came online just as the 2008 corn spike and credit freeze bankrupted a wave of US ethanol producers.
turn: The 2006 Whitehall sale, executed at the top of the hotel cycle two years before the crash.

s: POET is private and family-owned; company-disclosed scale is about $8B of annual revenue, 28 biorefineries and over 2 billion gallons a year
m: Modelled from disclosed production capacity at recent per-gallon ethanol plant transaction values, net of debt, times the Broin family's controlling ownership; no published figure exists
did: Took charge in 1987 of a foreclosed ethanol plant at Scotland, South Dakota that his father bought by mortgaging the family farm, and built it into POET, the world's largest biofuel producer: 28 biorefineries across seven states, more than two billion gallons a year and roughly 8 billion dollars of revenue, still entirely family-owned.
why: POET designed and built its own plants instead of buying turnkey ones, so each refinery cost less to erect and ran at higher yields than a competitor's, and it bought corn straight from the farmers surrounding each plant. The 2005 and 2007 renewable fuel standards then guaranteed a blending market by statute.
obst: The 2008 corn price spike and credit freeze bankrupted VeraSun and a dozen listed ethanol firms; POET survived because it was unlevered and private. Small-refinery exemptions granted after 2017 later destroyed several years of mandated blending demand at a stroke.
turn: The 2005 Energy Policy Act renewable fuel standard, which converted ethanol from an octane additive into a legally mandated market.

s: Long-standing press reporting on his privately held Budget Suites of America portfolio and the $350M-plus he has said he personally committed to Bigelow Aerospace
m: Inferred from the extended-stay portfolio and Las Vegas land, less disclosed self-funding of the aerospace venture; no rich-list figure is published
did: Built Budget Suites of America, a private chain of extended-stay apartment hotels across Las Vegas, Phoenix and Texas, then spent more than 350 million dollars of it founding Bigelow Aerospace in 1999 to build inflatable space habitats. His BEAM module has been bolted to the International Space Station since 2016.
why: Extended-stay units rent by the week to construction and casino workers who cannot pass a credit check for a lease, producing hotel-level rents on apartment-level cost and construction. Buying raw Las Vegas desert in the 1970s and holding it through four boom cycles did the rest.
obst: He licensed NASA's abandoned TransHab patents and then found no customer would buy a private space station: Bigelow Aerospace laid off its entire staff in March 2020 and has been dormant since, despite two free-flying prototypes that worked in 2006 and 2007.
turn: NASA's 2000 cancellation of TransHab, which let a Las Vegas landlord license inflatable-habitat technology the agency had already paid to develop.

s: Antero Resources DEF 14A: 10,572,536 AR shares, 3.2% of class, worth $401M at the $37.94 close of 21 Aug 2026, plus Antero Midstream stock; GuruFocus SEC-holdings valuation of $573M on 7 Aug 2026
m: Beneficial-ownership counts times fetched AR and AM prices; the two independent bases bracket $459M to $573M
did: A geologist who ran Barrett Resources and then Pennaco Energy before founding Antero Resources in Denver in 2002 with Glen Warren. Antero became the largest natural gas liquids producer in Appalachia and one of the biggest US gas producers; he moved to chairman emeritus in August 2025.
why: He leased Marcellus and Utica acreage in the wet gas window before anyone had proved shale gas would flow at scale, then built and kept Antero Midstream so the gathering and processing margin stayed inside the family of companies. Firm pipeline contracts moved his gas out of Appalachia while rivals sold into a glutted local market.
obst: He built and sold two companies, Barrett to Williams and Pennaco to Marathon, before shale worked at all. The 2019-2020 gas collapse drove Antero's stock under two dollars and forced asset sales and a distressed debt exchange to avoid default.
turn: The 2008 decision to sell the Barnett and Piceance positions and put everything into Appalachian wet gas.

s: Forbes estimate of $500-600 million made in 2018; no verified figure since, because his ADA position and IOHK equity are undisclosed
m: Dated third-party estimate retained rather than re-modelled; a token holding of unknown size cannot be marked honestly
did: One of the five original Ethereum co-founders and briefly its chief executive until he was forced out in 2014. He then co-founded IOHK with Jeremy Wood and built Cardano, a peer-reviewed proof-of-stake blockchain whose ADA token launched in 2017. He runs it from an 11,000-acre bison ranch near Wheatland, Wyoming.
why: Cardano was funded by a Japanese retail token sale rather than venture capital, so he was never diluted and never had a board. Shipping through formally verified academic papers gave the project an identity distinct from the Ethereum forks, and Wyoming then wrote the DAO and digital-asset statutes he had lobbied for.
obst: He was removed from Ethereum in 2014 with nothing to show for it. Cardano shipped smart contracts five years after promising them and was repeatedly dismissed as a ghost chain with no applications, and the SEC named ADA as an alleged unregistered security in its 2023 exchange cases.
turn: The 2017 ADA distribution and exchange listing, which turned an unfunded research shop into a top-ten token.

s: Boyd Gaming DEF 14A filed 20 Mar 2026: 6,280,547 shares, 8.34% of class; BYD closed $80.78 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed personal share count times fetched price, a floor that excludes private real estate; Forbes credits the wider Boyd family with more
did: A Las Vegas lawyer who put up his own savings in 1975 to open the California Hotel downtown with his father Sam, then built Boyd Gaming into 28 properties, took it public in 1993 and partnered with MGM to build Borgata. He is chairman emeritus at 95 and still on the payroll.
why: The California marketed almost exclusively to Hawaii, chartering flights and running its own Honolulu travel agency, which created a captive customer base no Strip operator competed for. Boyd then bought unloved locals casinos and regional riverboats at distressed prices in every subsequent downturn.
obst: The Echelon project was suspended in 2008 with billions committed and the site sat idle for years; the Coast Casinos and Ameristar acquisitions loaded the company with debt just before the financial crisis and the stock fell more than 90% in 2008 and 2009.
turn: The 1975 opening of the California Hotel with its Hawaii charter programme, which built a customer base 2,500 miles offshore.

s: Forbes 400 listing in 1998 at roughly $400M-plus; R.D. Offutt Farms and RDO Equipment remain family-held with roughly $3B of combined revenue
m: Dated Forbes 400 figure carried forward against current private-company scale; no current published figure exists
did: Mortgaged family land in 1968 to buy a John Deere dealership at Casselton, North Dakota, then built two businesses at once: R.D. Offutt Farms, the largest potato grower in the United States at roughly 190,000 acres and a principal french-fry supplier to McDonald's, and RDO Equipment, one of Deere's largest dealer groups.
why: Owning the dealerships and the farms together meant the equipment margin subsidised the crop and the crop justified the equipment volume. Growing potatoes under contract for processors rather than for the open market took the price volatility out of the riskiest row crop in America.
obst: The farms drew years of litigation and regulatory fights in Minnesota over irrigation permits and the conversion of pine forest into potato ground, and Deere's dealer consolidation repeatedly forced him to buy neighbouring dealers or be bought out himself.
turn: The 1970s shift from selling potatoes on the open market to contracting the entire crop to frozen-fry processors.

s: The Moyes family held about 39% of Swift at its 2007 take-private and roughly a tenth of Knight-Swift after the 2017 merger; they are absent from the April 2026 Knight-Swift proxy, so below 5%
m: Residual-stake inference from disclosed ownership history net of documented sales; no current published figure exists
did: Turned his father's small Arizona trucking outfit into Swift Transportation, the largest US truckload carrier, took it public in 1990, took it private again in a 2.7 billion dollar buyout he personally led in 2007, relisted it in 2010 and merged it with rival Knight Transportation in 2017 to create Knight-Swift.
why: Swift ran a dense terminal network across the southwest and hauled the Mexico-bound and return freight longer-haul carriers would not touch, then trained its own drivers in company schools once the binding constraint in trucking became people rather than trucks.
obst: He resigned as Swift's chief executive in 2005 after the SEC charged him over trades in another company's stock. His 2007 buyout closed weeks before freight volumes collapsed, and the margin loans secured on his Swift shares nearly forced a liquidation in 2009.
turn: The 2017 merger with Knight, which put a disciplined operator in charge of Swift's fleet and revalued the combined company.

s: Pluralsight DEF 14A, March 2020: 1,525,785 Class A and 14,373,295 Class C shares, 53.6% of voting power; Vista Equity's take-private closed April 2021 at $22.50 a share in cash
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times the announced cash merger price, before tax and option strike
did: Co-founded Pluralsight in Farmington, Utah in 2004 as an in-person developer training company, converted it to a video subscription library in 2007, bootstrapped for eight years before raising late-stage venture money, took it public in 2018 and sold it to Vista Equity Partners in April 2021 for 3.5 billion dollars.
why: Enterprise IT departments had to retrain staff on new frameworks faster than universities could teach them, and Pluralsight paid its authors royalties rather than salaries, so the catalogue grew with demand at almost no fixed cost. Selling seats to the CIO rather than to individual developers made it a renewable enterprise contract.
obst: The founders funded the company from their own consulting income for eight years. After the 2018 IPO Pluralsight missed billings guidance and the stock halved; Vista's leveraged buyout later defaulted and lenders took the company in 2024.
turn: The 2011 switch from selling courses one at a time to an all-you-can-watch enterprise subscription.

s: SEC Form 4 filings across his 1999-2019 DaVita tenure disclose his option exercises, sales and holdings at retirement; no rich-list figure is published
m: Inferred from disclosed insider sales and residual holdings; deliberately conservative because post-retirement disposals are not tracked
did: Took over Total Renal Care in 1999 when it was days from breaching its bank covenants, renamed it DaVita, moved it to Denver and ran it for twenty years into the largest US dialysis operator, treating roughly a third of American kidney patients across some 2,700 clinics.
why: Dialysis is a fixed-cost business where the binding constraint is chair utilisation, so consolidating clinics gave DaVita scale to negotiate drug prices and to hold commercial insurance rates far above what Medicare pays. A patient comes three times a week for life, which makes the revenue an annuity.
obst: He inherited a company with a going-concern qualification and no cash. DaVita later paid roughly 1.3 billion dollars settling federal whistleblower and anti-kickback cases over drug billing and patient referrals, and he was criticised for funding California ballot fights against dialysis price caps.
turn: The 2005 acquisition of Gambro Healthcare's US clinics, which doubled the company and made dialysis a duopoly with Fresenius.

s: Novell acquired WordPerfect Corporation in June 1994 for about $1.4B in stock; Ashton and co-founder Bruce Bastian were the controlling shareholders
m: Founder share of the disclosed merger consideration, heavily discounted for the subsequent fall in Novell stock and four decades of documented philanthropy
did: A BYU computer science professor who wrote a word processor for the Orem city government in 1979 with his student Bruce Bastian. WordPerfect took more than 80% of the corporate PC word-processing market in the 1980s, and they sold it to Novell in June 1994 for about 1.4 billion dollars in stock.
why: WordPerfect worked with every printer that existed, hundreds of drivers nobody else bothered to write, and shipped with free unlimited telephone support, which is what actually sold it to law firms and government offices. Function-key commands made trained secretaries fast and made switching expensive.
obst: They were late to Windows: the 1991 Windows version shipped buggy and two years behind Word, and the market was gone in about eighteen months. The Novell stock taken as consideration then fell sharply, and Novell resold WordPerfect to Corel for a fraction of the price in 1996.
turn: The 1982 decision to write printer drivers for every printer on the market, which made WordPerfect the only word processor that worked everywhere.

s: Extra Space Storage DEF 14A, April 2026: 874,197 shares, worth $128M at the $146.81 close of 21 Aug 2026, plus the 1995 sale of Megahertz to U.S. Robotics
m: Disclosed EXR share count times fetched price, plus an inferred residual from the Megahertz stock merger; deliberately conservative
did: Co-founded Megahertz Corporation in Utah in 1985, the maker of the PCMCIA modems that first put laptops online, and sold it to U.S. Robotics in 1995. He then backed Extra Space Storage and ran it as chief executive from 2009 to 2017, taking a regional operator into the second-largest US self-storage REIT.
why: Self-storage rents reset monthly, so a national operator can push rates on sitting tenants faster than inflation because moving out costs more than the increase. Extra Space grew mostly by managing other owners buildings for a fee, taking scale and acquisition rights without putting up capital.
obst: Megahertz shipped into a modem market where speeds doubled annually and inventory went obsolete in months. Extra Space then took heavy leverage buying Storage USA's portfolio in 2005 and had to carry that debt through the 2008 credit freeze.
turn: The 2009 launch of the third-party management platform, which let Extra Space add scale without buying the buildings.

s: Blackstone acquired APX Group (Vivint) for about $2B in 2012; NRG bought Vivint Smart Home for $2.8B at $12 a share in March 2023
m: Founder residual across two disclosed sale prices, net of the modest current holdings visible in his Form 4 history; deliberately conservative
did: Started selling home alarm contracts door to door as a BYU student in 1999, built APX Alarm into the second-largest US residential security company, renamed it Vivint in 2011, sold it to Blackstone for about 2 billion dollars in 2012, listed it via SPAC in 2020 and sold it again to NRG for 2.8 billion in 2023.
why: Vivint's summer sales army, thousands of students knocking doors on straight commission, acquired subscribers at a cost the incumbents retail and dealer channels could not match. The monitoring contracts it created were financeable assets that could be securitised to fund the next summer's hiring.
obst: The FTC and state regulators pursued the door-to-door channel over deceptive sales and credit-pull practices, and Vivint paid a 20 million dollar FTC settlement in 2021. The SPAC listing left the company carrying heavy subscriber-acquisition debt into a rising-rate market.
turn: The 2012 Blackstone buyout, which recapitalised a business whose whole model ran on borrowing against future contracts.

s: Zayo Group DEF 14A, September 2019: 5,073,372 shares, 2.1% of class; the Digital Colony and EQT take-private closed March 2020 at $35.00 a share in cash
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times the announced cash merger price, before tax
did: Founded Zayo Group in Boulder in 2007 to roll up dark fibre, bought 45 companies in twelve years, took it public in 2014 and sold it to Digital Colony and EQT in March 2020 for 14.3 billion dollars including debt, the largest take-private of that year.
why: Fibre already in the ground has near-zero marginal cost and a twenty-year life, so buying it below replacement cost out of distressed telecom estates and reselling capacity to carriers and data centres produced a spread that compounded with each deal. Bandwidth demand grew every year regardless of the economy.
obst: He had already lost most of a fortune once when ICG Communications went bankrupt in 2000. Zayo's serial acquisitions drew short-seller reports questioning its capitalisation of maintenance spend, and the stock halved in 2017 and 2018 before the buyout.
turn: The 2012 acquisition of AboveNet for 2.2 billion dollars, which gave Zayo metro fibre in the cities that actually mattered.

s: Oracle acquired RightNow Technologies for $1.5B in 2011 and Gianforte has said his proceeds exceeded $300M; Montana press and Forbes have since put him at roughly $180-210M
m: Disclosed sale proceeds less two decades of documented philanthropy and self-funded campaigns; third-party estimate
did: Founded RightNow Technologies in Bozeman in 1997 with his wife Susan, selling web-based customer service software on subscription years before anyone said SaaS; Oracle bought it for 1.5 billion dollars in 2011. He has been governor of Montana since 2021.
why: RightNow sold self-service knowledge bases to call centres whose economics ran on cost per contact, so every deflected phone call paid for the software directly. Running it from Bozeman meant engineers at half Silicon Valley wages and almost no attrition, which is why a subscription business survived three years without venture money.
obst: He bootstrapped for three years and was told repeatedly that no enterprise software company could be built in Montana. RightNow traded below its 2004 IPO price for years because investors penalised subscription revenue in favour of upfront licences.
turn: Oracle's October 2011 bid, made to plug the customer-service hole in its cloud stack against Salesforce.

s: Golden Entertainment DEF 14A: 6,548,788 shares, 24.8% of class; VICI Properties' acquisition closed 30 April 2026 with GDEN last trading at $28.55
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times the final trading price at the completed cash acquisition, before tax
did: Left Station Casinos in 2001 to build Golden Gaming, a Nevada route operator placing and servicing slot machines in taverns and grocery stores, reverse-merged it into Lakes Entertainment in 2015 to create Golden Entertainment, ran eight casinos and 73 taverns, and sold the company to VICI Properties in April 2026.
why: Nevada's restricted gaming licence lets a tavern hold fifteen slot machines and the route operator supplies and services them for a share of the win, a casino business with no casino to build and no hotel rooms to fill. Buying the taverns themselves later captured the food margin and the gaming split together.
obst: Route operators live on renewable location contracts a landlord can hand to a rival overnight. Covid closed every Nevada tavern in 2020, and the company had to sell its distributed-gaming division in 2023 to cut leverage.
turn: The 2015 reverse merger into Lakes Entertainment, which gave a private route operator a listed currency to buy casinos with.

s: Allegiant Travel DEF 14A filed 15 May 2026: 2,048,348 shares, 11.1% of class; ALGT closed $81.85 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Disclosed beneficial share count times fetched market price; excludes private holdings
did: Co-founded ValuJet in 1993, then bought the bankrupt Allegiant Air out of Chapter 11 in 2001 for about a million dollars and rebuilt it in Las Vegas as a leisure carrier flying second-hand MD-80s from small cities straight to Las Vegas, Orlando and Phoenix. Allegiant absorbed Sun Country in May 2026.
why: Allegiant flew routes no other airline served, two or three times a week, out of airports that paid subsidies to attract it, so it never competed on price with a network carrier and never flew a schedule it could not fill. Paying cash for twenty-year-old aircraft made ownership cost near zero and thin routes profitable.
obst: ValuJet's 1996 Everglades crash destroyed that airline and its reputation. Allegiant's ageing MD-80 fleet drew a 2018 network-television investigation into mid-air breakdowns, and its Sunseeker resort in Florida ran hundreds of millions over budget.
turn: The 2003 shift from selling seats to bundling hotel rooms and rental cars with the ticket, which made the airline a travel agency with planes.

s: Adobe acquired Omniture for $1.8B in 2009; his roughly 10% Domo stake is worth under $20M at DOMO's $3.80 close on 21 Aug 2026
m: Reported Omniture proceeds carried forward plus a marked-to-market Domo stake; third-party estimate of about $160M
did: Dropped out of BYU to start MyComputer.com in 1996, which became Omniture, the web analytics service that measured traffic for most of the Fortune 500; sold it to Adobe for 1.8 billion dollars in 2009 and immediately founded Domo in Utah, raising more than 700 million dollars for a business-intelligence dashboard that never repeated it.
why: Omniture sold analytics as a hosted service billed on traffic volume when everyone else sold log-analysis software on a licence, so its revenue grew automatically as its customers sites grew. Adobe needed measurement to sell a marketing suite and had nothing else to buy.
obst: Omniture nearly died twice in the dot-com bust and was refused funding repeatedly. Domo then burned more than a billion dollars of capital, listed in 2018 far below its last private round, and has traded under five dollars since.
turn: The 2007 acquisition of Visual Sciences, which consolidated web analytics under Omniture and set up the Adobe sale two years later.

s: Forbes, November 2024: at least $100 million, built from his OGE Form 278e disclosure; his 2001 Microsoft consideration was more than 1.7 million shares
m: Government ethics disclosure ranges plus the disclosed merger consideration; Forbes notes the true figure may be higher because family trusts are not reportable
did: Mortgaged farmland he inherited near Arthur, North Dakota in 1983 to buy into Great Plains Software, an accounting package for small businesses, ran it as chief executive, took it public in 1997 and sold it to Microsoft in 2001 for 1.1 billion dollars in stock. Governor of North Dakota to 2024 and US Interior Secretary since 2025.
why: Great Plains sold only through a channel of accountants and value-added resellers, never direct, so thousands of local bookkeepers had a commercial reason to recommend it and to carry the support burden themselves. That channel was the asset Microsoft actually bought, because it reached small businesses Microsoft could not.
obst: He put inherited farmland at risk to fund a software company in a state with no software industry and no venture capital, then had to rebuild the entire product for Windows in the mid-1990s while a reseller channel that made money on DOS resisted the change.
turn: Microsoft's December 2000 all-stock offer, agreed months before the software market repriced.

s: Forbes, August 2025: a fortune of roughly $100 million on entering the cabinet, including a 1.6% Liberty Energy stake worth about $50M that ethics rules required him to sell
m: Published Forbes estimate built from his OGE Form 278e disclosure; SEC-derived third-party estimates run higher
did: Founded Pinnacle Technologies in 1992 and commercialised the fracture mapping that let operators see where a hydraulic fracture actually went, then founded Liberty Resources and Liberty Energy in Denver in 2011 and built one of the largest North American pressure-pumping companies. Sworn in as US Energy Secretary in February 2025.
why: Liberty entered pressure pumping with its own engineering rather than as a fleet renter, so it designed the frac job and was paid for the result instead of by the hour. It then bought Schlumberger's entire North American fracturing business in 2020 for stock, at the bottom of the cycle, and came out of covid as the scale player.
obst: Liberty listed in January 2018 straight into the shale service collapse; the 2020 oil crash took the stock under two dollars and the dividend was suspended weeks after it agreed to absorb Schlumberger's loss-making frac fleet.
turn: The August 2020 all-stock deal to take over Schlumberger's North American fracturing business at the cycle low.
